This page goes with **Chapter 16, Figured Bass** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/FiguredBass.html). Read each section there
first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It builds on the Roman numerals of [Chapter 7](roman-numerals.qmd) and the
seventh chords of [Chapter 8](seventh-chords.qmd), where inversions were written /3rd, /5th and /7th. From this chapter on, the
book writes them with figures instead.

Every drill has **Settings**, and is also on the [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd) page. Click a section's heading to fold it; the
list on the right jumps to a section.

## 16.1 Historical context

In the Baroque era (roughly 1600–1750) a keyboard or lute player often read only a **bass line with numbers** under it, and filled in
the chords. That shorthand is **figured bass** (also called thoroughbass). The numbers are **intervals above the bass note**, counted
**in the key signature**. They say which notes to play, not how to space them, so players chose their own voicings, the way a pianist
reading lead-sheet symbols does today. Modern editions often "realize" the figures: they write the chords out.
Today theory classes use figured bass mostly as a shorthand for inversions, written after a Roman numeral.
[Read 16.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/FiguredBassHistoricalContext.html)

::: {.rn-quiz}
<figure><figcaption>Handel, Recorder Sonata in A minor, HWV 362, I. Larghetto (the book's Figure 16.1.3)</figcaption>
<iframe class="dr-yt" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/ljj6URbK8Xg?start=0&end=13&rel=0" title="Handel, Recorder Sonata in A minor, HWV 362" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe></figure>
:::

**Counting an interval:** count letter names from the bass up to the note, counting both ends. From G up to E is G A B C D E, six
letters: a **6th**. Octaves don't matter (a 13th still counts as a 6), and neither does which voice has the note.

## 16.2 Figured bass inversion symbols

Pick a chord and a bass note. Each bracket on the staff runs from the bass to one of the notes above it, with the interval it makes.
The figures under the bass are in the colour of the chord member they land on: <span style="color:#d1495b">root</span>,
<span style="color:#2e86ab">3rd</span>, <span style="color:#3c9d5d">5th</span>, <span style="color:#c77d0a">7th</span>. Faint figures in
brackets are understood but not written. Hover over a line of the explanation to light up its note.
[Read 16.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/FiguredBassInversionSymbols.html)

<div class="fb-explorer" data-key="C" data-mode="major" data-chord="0" data-inv="2"></div>

The symbols, from the book's Figures 16.2.1–2:

| Bass note | Triad | Every interval above the bass | Seventh chord | Every interval above the bass |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Root | (none) | 5/3 | 7 | 7/5/3 |
| 3rd | 6 | 6/3 | 6/5 | 6/5/3 |
| 5th | 6/4 | 6/4 | 4/3 | 6/4/3 |
| 7th | | | 4/2 | 6/4/2 |

The short forms keep just the numbers that tell one position from another. Four rules from 16.2:

- The figures go **after** the Roman numeral (I64, V65), not under the bass as in Baroque scores.
- Compare the slash labels of earlier chapters: I/3rd = **I6**, I/5th = **I64**, V7/3rd = **V65**, V7/5th = **V43**, V7/7th = **V42**.
- Since 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2 only ever mean seventh chords, an inverted seventh chord **drops the 7**: V65, not V7 65.
- The quality signs stay: **IM43** (a major seventh chord), **viiø65**, **vii°42**.

Given the numeral, write the notes, lowest first:

<div class="drill" data-ex="fbwrite" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&kind=both&inv=inv"></div>

Without Roman numerals: count up from the lowest note and choose the figure.

<div class="drill" data-ex="fbfig" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&kind=both&clef=treble,bass"></div>

### What the numbers mean, the other way round

A Baroque player sees a bass note and figures and works out the notes: count each interval up from the bass, using the key
signature's sharps and flats. In C major, **6/4 over D** is D, then a 4th up (G), then a 6th up (B): the G chord with its 5th in the
bass. Type every note, bass first:

<div class="drill" data-ex="fbreal" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&kind=triads&show=staff"></div>

With seventh chords, and in minor keys (the notes come from the key signature, so V in a minor key comes out minor here; a real
figured bass would add an accidental to raise the leading tone, as the explorer shows):

<div class="drill" data-ex="fbreal" data-settings="mode=both&most=4&kind=both&show=staff"></div>

## 16.3 The cadential six-four chord

The **I64** that so often comes just before **V** at a cadence is called the **cadential six-four**. The bass stays on scale degree 5
for both chords, and the 6th and 4th above it fall to a 5th and a 3rd: really V with two notes delayed. So the book counts it as
**dominant** function, like the V after it. Earlier chapters called it I/5th.
[Read 16.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/TheCadentialSixFourChord.html)

::: {.rn-quiz}
<figure><figcaption>Mozart, Piano Sonata K. 331, I (the book's Figure 16.3.1)</figcaption>
<iframe class="dr-yt" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/vp_h649sZ9A?start=14&end=25&rel=0" title="Mozart, Piano Sonata K. 331" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe></figure>

<figure><figcaption>Key and Smith, "The Star-Spangled Banner" (the book's Figure 16.3.2)</figcaption>
<iframe class="dr-yt" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/LGvW6jHUHiY?start=77&end=93&rel=0" title="The Star-Spangled Banner" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe></figure>
:::

In the explorer, choose **I**, then **5th 6/4**, then **V**, **root 5/3**: the bass doesn't move; the C and E above it step down to B
and D.

## 16.4 Other six-four chords

A six-four chord (the 5th in the bass) turns up in only four situations in classical music:

- **Cadential:** I64 before V over the same bass note (16.3).
- **Passing:** the bass moves by step through three notes, and the middle chord is a six-four (I – V64 – I6, the bass going 1–2–3).
- **Pedal:** the bass repeats one note three times, and the middle chord is a six-four (I – IV64 – I over a held tonic).
- **Melodic bass:** the bass has the tune, and when the tune lands on the chord's 5th the chord is a six-four.

[Read 16.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/OtherOccurrencesofSixFourChords.html)

Four chords, the second a six-four. Which kind? Watch (or hear) the bass:

<div class="drill" data-ex="sixfour" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&show=both"></div>

By ear, and in minor keys too:

<div class="drill" data-ex="sixfour" data-settings="mode=both&most=3&show=ear"></div>

## 16.5 Additional information

In Baroque scores you'll sometimes see every interval written out (6/5/3 for 6/5, 6/4/3 for 4/3). The short symbols are
abbreviations of those; the table in 16.2 gives both. Figures in real music can also carry **accidentals** for notes outside the key
signature, such as the raised leading tone in a minor key. An accidental with no number beside it means the 3rd above the bass.
Roman-numeral analysis leaves these accidentals out. To see one, set the explorer to a minor key and choose **V**.
[Read 16.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/FiguredBassAdditionalInformation.html)

## For teachers

- **Links with your settings:** open a drill's **Settings**, then **Copy a link with these settings**. Add `&lock=1` for a test, `&count=20` for a score.
  The explorer takes `data-key`, `data-mode`, `data-chord` (0 = tonic), `data-seventh="1"` and `data-inv` (0–3) to open on a given chord.
- **Answers accepted:** the figures (I64, V65, IM43, viiø42) and the older slash labels (I/5th, V7/3rd) both count. An inverted seventh chord
  written with the 7 (V765) is not accepted, following 16.2.
- **Chords drilled:** in minor, the book's common set (i ii° III iv V VI VII vii°, and i7 iiø7 IIIM7 iv7 V7 VIM7 vii°7).
- **Realizing figures** uses the key signature only, as 16.1 describes; the minor-key V comes out minor there, and the explorer shows the
  accidental a Baroque figure would add (a lone accidental for the 3rd).
- **The six-four drill's voicings** are this site's own: IV – I64 – V – I (cadential), I – V64 – I6 – IV (passing, with a voice exchange
  between bass and alto), I – IV64 – I – V (pedal). The melodic-bass six-four is not drilled.
- **Checked:** `node tests/lessons/figured-drill.test.js` generates about nine thousand questions and checks each by its own arithmetic: the figure
  is read from the sounding notes, realized notes count up the right number of letters in the key signature, each six-four type has the
  book's bass shape (`NEG=1` breaks the engine on purpose and must fail).
- **Not from the book (unverified against a source here):** two common-practice statements are the site's own: that a lone accidental in
  a figure means the 3rd above the bass (16.5 only shows that figures can carry accidentals), and that the cadential six-four's 6th and
  4th fall to a 5th and 3rd over the same bass (16.3 says only that it has dominant function).
- **Videos:** the book's YouTube links with its start and end times, each checked against YouTube.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
